query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Reducing the fraction of Hf in the HfMoTaTiZr alloy and compensating by keeping the concentrations of the other constituent elements unchanged will lower the overall density while preserving the alloy's high-strength performance at room temperature and near 1000 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr high‐entropy alloy with a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³ and high strength at both room temperature and elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Lower the Hf content (e.g., reducing the Hf atomic ratio by nearly 50%) in the alloy composition while keeping the proportions of Mo, Ta, Ti, and Zr constant.
generation.conditions: Mechanical tests performed at room temperature and at elevated temperatures up to approximately 1000 °C; loading conditions consistent with tensile or compressive strength measurements.
generation.structural_mediator: A reduction in heavy Hf atoms is expected to decrease the average atomic mass and density without adversely altering the single-phase BCC structure. Controlled microstructure (grain size and phase stability) is maintained by the presence of the other refractory elements.
generation.mechanism: Since Hf is one of the highest density constituents, reducing its fraction lowers the overall mass per unit volume. Prior evidence suggests that decreasing Hf content can even favorably affect strength. By preserving the ratios of other high-melting, mechanically robust elements, the high-temperature stability and strength remain largely unaffected.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy will exhibit a notable reduction in density from the as‐cast state while maintaining comparable yield/ultimate strength at room temperature and at approximately 1000 °C. There may be a slight improvement or no significant loss in strength due to microstructural stability.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics of as‐cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr including density of ~10.21 g/cm³ and high strength (σ comparable to similar HEAs, e.g., ~970 MPa at room temperature).
generation.boundary: Temperature range from room temperature to approximately 1000 °C under mechanical loading conditions typical for tensile or compression tests. The intervention is assumed to be effective as long as the phase remains single BCC and grain coarsening is controlled.
generation.uncertainty: It is uncertain how sensitive the microstructure might be to the Hf reduction alone without additional processing (e.g., grain refinement by LMD) and whether any trade-offs in elastic modulus or long‐term thermal stability might occur.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce a batch of the modified alloy with a reduced Hf content (e.g., Hf fraction reduced by ~50% relative to the equiatomic composition) while keeping Mo, Ta, Ti, and Zr concentrations unchanged. Process the alloy under the same as‐cast conditions. Conduct density measurements along with mechanical tests (tensile/compressive) at room temperature and at 1000 °C. Compare the measured values to the baseline performance of the as‐cast equiatomic alloy.
measurements: Tensile strength and yield strength at room temperature
Tensile strength and yield strength at 1000 °C
Microstructural analysis (grain size, phase identification via XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with reduced Hf does not show a statistically significant reduction in density relative to 10.21 g/cm³, or if the room temperature and/or high-temperature (1000 °C) strength values drop significantly (e.g., more than a 10-15% decrease) compared to the as‐cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr baseline, then the hypothesis is rejected.

## Abstract
High-entropy alloy (HEA) is a new type of multi-principal alloy material and the Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr HEAs have attracted more and more attention from researchers due to their high melting point, special plasticity, and excellent corrosion resistance. In this paper, in order to reduce the density of the alloy and maintain the strength of the Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr HEAs, the effects of high-density elements Hf and Ta on the properties of HEAs were explored for the first time based on molecular dynamics simulations. A low-density and high-strength Hf0.25NbTa0.25TiZr HEA suitable for laser melting deposition was designed and formed. Studies have shown that the decrease in the proportion of Ta element reduces the strength of HEA, while the decrease in Hf element increases the strength of HEA. The simultaneous decrease in the ratio of Hf and Ta elements reduces the elastic modulus and strength of HEA and leads to the coarsening of the alloy microstructure. The application of laser melting deposition (LMD) technology refines the grains and effectively solves the coarsening problem.
